intro: You are standing in Göreme Open Air Museum, a rock settlement in Nevşehir province whose story belongs to the 10th–12th century AD. All around you, monasteries and churches have been cut straight into the tuff. And somewhere among them waits the Dark Church, whose frescoes are among the best-preserved Byzantine paintings anywhere. Shall we step into this world of rock?
history: Why here? The answer lies in the stone itself. Volcanic tuff is soft enough to dig with a pick, yet it hardens once cut. That is why, from the tenth century on, the Göreme valley became a landscape of monasteries, as churches, refectories and cells were hollowed out one by one. Some were painted on plaster, others straight onto the rock. And the Dark Church? It kept its colours because only a single small window lets the light in.
structure-1: Next stop: the Dark Church. It is not cut into a fairy chimney but into a great mass of tuff, as part of a monastery: a small courtyard, a two-storey front carved with doors and blind arches, a refectory, and up a curving stair the frescoed church itself. Many other churches here are cut into the fairy chimneys: cones of soft tuff under caps of harder rock, with carved fronts of doors, windows and blind arcades. Göreme has more painted churches than anywhere else in Cappadocia; most of the frescoes are of the 10th and 11th centuries.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the Dark Church, the Buckle Church and the Apple Church. Then look for the Snake Church, and end your walk at the Nunnery.
facts: Did you know? The frescoes of the Dark Church emerged from a restoration that took many years to lift away the soot. The church takes its name from its single small window: because so little light gets in, its frescoes are the most vividly coloured in Cappadocia. Here is another curiosity. Most of the rock churches were carved with columns and arches that hold nothing up. Inside solid rock they serve no structural purpose at all; they are there so that the space would look like a real church. And one last detail: the blue of the Buckle Church was made from lapis lazuli, a stone so costly at the time that it was brought from very far away.
outro: This brings our journey through Göreme Open Air Museum to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have waited for centuries; let them keep waiting for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
